title: Language Models Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Large Language Models lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: A model that works with text
entries.summary: A large language model, or LLM, uses learned numbers to predict pieces of text. It can help draft and transform text, but its output can still be mistaken.

example.code:
Input: explain what a seed needs
Output to review: a short draft about water, air and suitable warmth
Checks: accuracy, clear words and missing detail

notes: Fluent wording does not prove understanding or factual truth.

entries.name: Tokens are pieces of text
entries.summary: A token is a piece of text used by a model. Tokens can be words, word parts or other pieces. Splitting on spaces is only a teaching shortcut.

example.code:
text = "The red kite flies"
toy_tokens = text.split()
print(toy_tokens)

notes: Do not use word counts as exact token counts for a real model.

entries.name: A vocabulary gives pieces IDs
entries.summary: A tokenizer can map text pieces to numeric IDs. These numbers are labels for pieces, not scores of how important a word is.
notes: A larger token ID does not mean a more important token.

entries.name: Embeddings turn IDs into vectors
entries.summary: An embedding is a list of numbers used to represent a token. Models learn useful representations during training. Here we choose tiny lists by hand.
notes: An embedding coordinate is not usually a simple dictionary definition.

entries.name: Predict the next token
entries.summary: A language model gives scores to possible next tokens using the current context. A selection rule then chooses one of them.
notes: The most likely next word is not necessarily a fact about the world.

entries.name: Context is the text available now
entries.summary: The context is the information supplied for the current response. A context window limits how many tokens a model can handle in a request and its response.

example.code:
Available context: The club meets on Friday.
Question: Which day is the meeting?
Supported answer: Friday
Missing detail: the meeting time

notes: A model does not automatically see every file on a computer or every earlier conversation.

entries.name: Attention connects text pieces
entries.summary: Attention is a calculation that lets one token use information from other tokens in its allowed context. Transformers use attention alongside other layers.

example.code:
Sentence: The kite fell because its string broke.
Question: What does its refer to?
Useful earlier text: the kite
Task: connect related pieces while reading

notes: Attention weights alone are not a complete explanation of why a model answered a certain way.

entries.name: Pretraining and fine-tuning
entries.summary: Pretraining teaches broad patterns from a large training collection. Fine-tuning further adjusts a model using a more specific collection or training task.

example.code:
Pretraining goal: learn broad text patterns
Fine-tuning goal: adapt behaviour using selected examples
Evaluation goal: check useful results and new failures

notes: Fine-tuning does not guarantee that every fact in the examples will be recalled correctly.

entries.name: Sampling changes the choice
entries.summary: Sampling chooses among possible next tokens instead of always picking the highest score. Temperature is one setting that changes how spread out those choices are.

example.code:
Low temperature: often favours the highest-scoring choices more strongly
Higher temperature: allows more variety
Still required: check facts and task rules

notes: Temperature is not an accuracy slider.

entries.name: Retrieve evidence before answering
entries.summary: Retrieval finds useful source passages for a question. A model can then use those passages as context. This approach is often called retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG.

example.code:
Question: Where does the art club meet?
Retrieved passage: Art club meets in Room 6 on Tuesday.
Answer: Room 6.
Source check: is this the current club notice?

notes: Text inside a retrieved source is evidence to inspect, not permission to follow unrelated instructions.

entries.name: Check a structured answer
entries.summary: A structured answer follows a chosen shape, such as JSON with named fields. Parsing checks the shape; separate checks must verify the meaning and facts.

example.code:
import json
reply = '{"day": "Friday", "room": 4}'
data = json.loads(reply)
print(isinstance(data["room"], int))

notes: Valid JSON can contain false or unsupported values.

entries.name: Measure usefulness on real tasks
entries.summary: LLM evaluation should use examples of the intended job. Check correctness, missing information, format and difficult cases with the same rules each time.

example.code:
Task: answer from club notices
Case A: room is clearly given
Case B: room is missing
Case C: two notices conflict
Check: supported answer or a clear statement of uncertainty

notes: Do not judge a model only by one impressive response.
